newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos says no crackdown on anti-APEC protests.
newsitem.headline: Ramos says no crackdown on anti-APEC protests.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday the arrest of a top Filipino leftist was not a crackdown on anti-APEC protests but admitted the seizure of the man two weeks before the APEC summit was poorly timed.

Filemon Lagman, chairman of a workers' group that the military has linked to alleged communist-inspired plots to disrupt the November 25 summit, was arrested on Tuesday while meeting union officials in a hotel in Manila's suburbs.
The labour alliance BMP (Coalition of Filipino Workers), headed by Lagman, said the arrest was reminiscent of "fascist attacks" during the rule of late president Ferdinand Marcos.
"The move might be misconstrued as a crackdown on anti-APEC protests but the case is a police matter and in no way related to APEC," Ramos told a meeting with his cabinet and Senate leaders.

Ramos, however, admitted that Lagman's arrest, less than two weeks before the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit, was "very, very untimely and unfortunate", a presidential palace news release said.
"I agree with your observation that the timing is not so good but if these are things that have to be done in order to protect the greater public interest, so be it," Ramos told the meeting.
Ramos denied at a news conference leftist allegations he had ordered Lagman's arrest.

"Please understand that the administration, the president ... would be the last people to undermine their own efforts to create the most positive, most favourable, the most hospitable atmosphere on the eve of our hosting of APEC," he said.
A BMP statement said Lagman's arrest would only heighten protests against the APEC summit to be held on November 25 at nearby Subic Bay.
The arrest "drops the dangling sword of fascist repression reminiscent of (Marcos's) martial law years," it said.
Military sources said more arrests of leftists loomed ahead.

They said Lagman, who is being held at military intelligence headquarters, was one of six leftists being hunted for alleged involvement in the 1992 killing of a Manila policeman by a communist hit-squad. The five others remain at large.

Opposition to APEC among leftists rose on Wednesday as 4,000 members of another leftist group marched to the presidential palace and the U.S. embassy to denounce the summit, to be attended by President Bill Clinton and other regional leaders.
They said the APEC goal of trade liberalisation would only allow developed member economies to dominate less advanced members.
Analysts said Lagman's arrest and a government threat to take over major local companies threatened by strikes showed Manila's determination to provide tight security for APEC leaders.

"The state has other measures, like taking over vital industries," Justice Secretary Teofisto Guingona told reporters, referring to government options to counter strike threats at the hotel, transportation and telecommunication sectors.
Those sectors will provide key services to the summit and ministerial meeting preceding it.
"The government is pulling all the stops to ensure security for APEC," said Alex Magno, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines.
"It's a warning shot across the bow of the demonstrators, that they can't get too far," analyst Teodoro Benigno said of Lagman's arrest.
